name: esp32-c3-adblock
cost: Free, plus an ESP32-C3 board (about $2 per the README)
works_with: ESP32-C3 boards with 4 MB flash (tested on a C3 SuperMini). Classic ESP32 4 MB boards also build. Built and flashed with PlatformIO
short: A Pi-hole style DNS ad blocker that runs on a cheap ESP32-C3 board with no PSRAM.
what: Firmware that turns an ESP32-C3 into a DNS sinkhole. It stores the blocklist as sorted 40-bit hashes in flash, so 140,000+ domains fit in about 0.7 MB and use about 50 KB of RAM. Blocked domains get 0.0.0.0, and everything else is forwarded to an upstream resolver.
who: Tinkerers with an ESP32 board who want network-wide ad blocking on cheap hardware, and who can flash firmware with PlatformIO. Skip it if you want a polished appliance or need TLS on the dashboard, which this chip doesn't run.
needs: An ESP32-C3 board with 4 MB flash (no PSRAM needed) and a stable USB power source
A current PlatformIO (the VSCode extension, or pip install -U platformio in a venv). The README says the distro/apt package is too old

steps.title: Create your secrets file
steps.text: Set real WEB_USER, WEB_PASS and OTA_PASS values in src/secrets.h. WiFi details are optional because there is a setup portal.

steps.title: Build the blocklist
steps.text: The default is StevenBlack base plus Hagezi Light, about 100k entries. You can pass your own URLs or files after the output name.

steps.title: Flash the firmware and the blocklist over USB
steps.text: This is the only USB flash. Later updates go over WiFi.
steps.code:
pio run -t upload
pio run -t uploadfs

steps.title: Watch it boot and open the dashboard
steps.text: If it can't connect to WiFi, join the C3-AdBlock-XXXX access point from your phone and pick your network.

steps.title: Point your DNS at it
steps.text: Set a device's DNS to the board's IP, or add it as a secondary resolver behind your main DNS.

try.label: From the README
try.text:
dig @<c3-ip> doubleclick.net   # -> 0.0.0.0  (blocked)
dig @<c3-ip> github.com        # -> real IP  (forwarded)

watch: Change the placeholder passwords in src/secrets.h. With the example values the device still boots, and its dashboard and OTA passwords are public in the repo.
The dashboard is plain HTTP with Basic Auth. The README says anyone who can sniff your LAN can read those credentials.
The WiFi setup access point is open (unencrypted), so the WiFi password you type there is only as safe as that local radio link during setup.
The device sits in the path of every DNS query on your network. Anyone who can reflash it controls your DNS, which is why the passwords matter.
Remote auto-update pulls a blocklist from a URL on a schedule. The README offers one rebuilt weekly by GitHub Actions in this repo.
With 4 MB flash, firmware OTA leaves room for about 250k domains. Larger lists need the single-app partition table and no firmware OTA.
The Linux ModemManager fix in the README runs sudo commands and adds a udev rule. Read them before running.
